claim: King Fung Construction Work Co. Ltd. claims against Yip Kwai Chor for repayment of $2.5 million, and against Yip Kwai Chor and SING YIP CONSTRUCTION ENGINEERING LTD. for various losses arising from alleged improper performance of contracts.
requested_remedy: King Fung Construction Work Co. Ltd. claims against Yip Kwai Chor for repayment of $2.5 million, and against Yip Kwai Chor and SING YIP CONSTRUCTION ENGINEERING LTD. for various losses arising from alleged improper performance of contracts.
parties: Plaintiff: King Fung Construction Work Co. Ltd.
Defendant: Yip Kwai Chor (1st Defendant); SING YIP CONSTRUCTION ENGINEERING LTD. (2nd Defendant)

facts.F1: King Fung Construction Work Co. Ltd. was formed on March 9, 2001, by Mr. Lau Kai Yam.
facts.F2: The company took on several sub-contracts, including ones at Ma On Shan and King’s Park, worth tens of millions of dollars.
facts.F3: Mr. Lau Kai Yam and Mr. Yip Kwai Chor entered into a business co-operation in May 2002, with Mr. Yip becoming a 30% shareholder in King Fung Construction Work Co. Ltd.
facts.F4: Mr. Yip's reliability and performance were called into question, with Mr. Lau alleging that he did not contribute capital to the business and performed poorly on certain contracts.
facts.F5: A series of loans were made by Mr. Lau to Mr. Yip, totaling $2.5 million.
facts.F6: Mr. Yip became involved in the Mainland in October 2003, and his connections led to him being detained for several months.
facts.F7: The disputed contracts, Kam Chin Village and Hang Hau, were sub-contracted to SING YIP CONSTRUCTION ENGINEERING LTD. at a 10% profit margin.
facts.F8: King Fung Construction Work Co. Ltd. took over the two contracts after Mr. Yip's detention and incurred significant expenses.
facts.F9: The total amounts claimed by King Fung Construction Work Co. Ltd. are: $2.5 million (personal loan), $3,247,828 (amounts advanced to SING YIP CONSTRUCTION ENGINEERING LTD.), and $5,647,441 (excess amount paid by King Fung Construction Work Co. Ltd.).
facts.F10: There is no written document evidence of Mr. Yip's suretyship.

claim: Declaration of entitlement in equity to be relieved against the forfeiture by the Crown of her interest in Castle Peak Town Lot No. 12 and an order vacating the Memorial of Re-entry
requested_remedy: Declaration of entitlement in equity to be relieved against the forfeiture by the Crown of her interest in Castle Peak Town Lot No. 12 and an order vacating the Memorial of Re-entry
parties: Plaintiff: The Plaintiff ( Name not specified )

facts.F1: Under an agreement dated 2nd April 1970, the Crown granted the plaintiff Castle Peak Town Lot No. 12 for 99 years less three days from 1st July 1898.
facts.F2: The agreement had a Building Covenant requiring the plaintiff to complete a two-storeyed factory building on the site within four years from the commencement date, i.e., by 1st July 1972.
facts.F3: The plaintiff sought financing from the Hongkong Chinese Bank Ltd. for an eight-storeyed factory, which was not approved by the bank.
facts.F4: The plaintiff's plans for the eight-storeyed factory were not approved until August 1971, and the District Commissioner, New Territories expressed concern over the development of the site in February 1972.
facts.F5: The Crown sent a letter to the plaintiff in March 1972 reminding her of the Building Covenant and the need for immediate development.
facts.F6: The plaintiff's daughter met with Mr. Dixon in July 1972, and it was alleged that he suggested reverting to the original two-storeyed building and promised approval within 28 days.
facts.F7: Plans for the two-storeyed factory were submitted in September 1972 but not approved until April 1973, by which time the four-year period had expired.
facts.F8: By Gazette Notification 1506 of 15th June 1973, the Crown published its Memorial of Re-entry, and the plaintiff's interest was forfeited.
facts.F9: The Crown demanded payment of the 5th instalment of the premium due under the Agreement on 16th March 1974, which the plaintiff paid on 25th March 1974.
facts.F10: The court found the plaintiff's evidence not credible and that she had wilfully breached the Building Covenant.
facts.F11: The plaintiff's delay in complying with the Building Covenant was a wilful one.
facts.F12: The plaintiff had fabricated excuses for non-compliance.
facts.F13: There were clear and wilful breaches of more than one covenant, similar to the case of Shiloh Spinners Ltd. v. Harding.

reference_issues: Whether the plaintiff is entitled to equitable relief against forfeiture for breach of the Building Covenant.
Whether the Crown's demand and receipt of the 5th instalment of the premium due under the Agreement after the Memorial of Re-entry amounted to a waiver or relinquishment of its right of re-entry.

Clause 9 of the agreement

Section 15(1) of the Building Ordinance

claim: damages for breach of contract
requested_remedy: damages for breach of contract

facts.F1: The plaintiff Mr Wong Leung Wing was the sole proprietor of Express Printing and Stationery Supplies from 1983 until 1991.
facts.F2: From 1983 until 1988, the plaintiff carried out a number of printing contracts for the defendant in Hong Kong.
facts.F3: On the 15th August 1985, the plaintiff entered into a contract for one year with the defendant to print cancellation bulletins.
facts.F4: The contract was renewed on the 15th May 1986 for two years and again for a further period of two years on the 15th November 1988, expiring on the 31st December 1990.
facts.F5: When the contract with the plaintiff was renewed in November 1988, Mr Fellman, a Vice-President of the defendant, was responsible for obtaining quotations for the printing of the cancellation bulletins.
facts.F6: Mr Antony Fung was employed by the defendant as a manager under Mr Fellman and liaised with Mr Wong in connection with the requirements of the defendant for the printing of the cancellation bulletins.
facts.F7: On the 22nd August 1988, Mr Wong wrote to the defendant with regard to a renewal of the contract and requested a revision of the previous pricing arrangement on the grounds of an increase in mailing costs and additional handling charges.
facts.F8: It is alleged by the defendant that the grounds for the increase were spurious and were made as a result of a collusive agreement between Mr Wong and Mr Fung.
facts.F9: Mr Fung left the employ of the defendant in March 1989.
facts.F10: On the 24th July 1989, Messrs Fred Kan & Co., solicitors, wrote a letter to the defendant on behalf of Mr Fung informing them that Mr Wong had assigned all his rights under the contract with the defendant to Mr Fung.
facts.F11: The letter reads that the assignment was entered into to secure the performance by Mr Wong of his obligations under a Promissory Note dated 9th day of June, 1989.
facts.F12: The defendant terminated the contract with the plaintiff on the 13th September 1989.
facts.F13: The ICAC reported to have carried out investigations, however, no charge has been preferred against Mr Wong although the investigations are still continuing.
facts.F14: Mr Wong had desperately wanted to retain the contract which was his main source of income.
facts.F15: Mr Wong contended that it was necessary for a solicitor to draw up a contract for the sale of paper when it had never been drawn up in this manner before.
facts.F16: There was an instance where Mr Wong and Mr Fung were talking at the same time when Mr Wu was explaining the contents of the promissory note.

lawsuit_type: action for damages for breach of contract
reference_issues: Whether Mr Wong inflated the price of the contract as a result of a collusive agreement with Mr Fung to obtain the contract and thereby enable him to pay bribes to Mr Fung.

claim: claims for a declaration that the Defendant wrongly terminated the Plaintiff's appointment as manager, damages for breach of contract, and for payment of $396,861.50 being monies owed to the Plaintiff by the Defendant prior to the termination of the parties' agreement
requested_remedy: claims for a declaration that the Defendant wrongly terminated the Plaintiff's appointment as manager, damages for breach of contract, and for payment of $396,861.50 being monies owed to the Plaintiff by the Defendant prior to the termination of the parties' agreement
parties: Plaintiff: ROTH & SONS ESTATES MANAGEMENT LIMITED
Defendant: THE INCORPORATED OWNERS OF CARSON MANSION, KING'S ROAD

facts.F1: The Plaintiff was incorporated in Hong Kong and carried on the business of building management.
facts.F2: The Defendant was the owner of a composite building known as Carson Mansion, which was incorporated under the Multi-Storey Buildings (Owners Incorporation) Ordinance.
facts.F3: The parties entered into a Deed of Mutual Covenant dated 20 July 1979 and a further Deed of Mutual Covenant dated 8 April 1980.
facts.F4: The Defendant appointed the Plaintiff as the manager of the Shopping Centre on 6 August 1987, and the Plaintiff served in that capacity until it was re-appointed in 1992.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff's appointment as manager was under a fresh agreement dated 1 January 1992, which provided for automatic renewal for another year unless notice was given one month prior to the expiration of the contract.
facts.F6: The Defendant did not give notice to terminate the contract at the end of 1993, and the Plaintiff's appointment as manager was renewed until 31 December 1994, with an increase in the management fee from $9,000 to $10,000 per month.
facts.F7: No notice was given to terminate the contract at the end of 1994, and the Plaintiff contended that its appointment as manager was extended for a further year until 31 December 1995.
facts.F8: The Defendant contended that the automatic renewal provisions only applied for one year and that the Plaintiff's appointment as manager continued on a monthly basis without renewal.
facts.F9: The Defendant terminated the Plaintiff's appointment on 15 March 1995, purporting to do so forthwith without compensation, but failed to comply with the provisions of the Seventh Schedule of the Building Management Ordinance requiring at least three months' notice.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff claimed damages for wrongful termination of the contract, including payment for services rendered and reimbursement of expenses incurred prior to termination.
facts.F11: The Defendant alleged that the Plaintiff had breached its duties and obligations under the contract, but failed to establish this through evidence.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff was employed on a monthly basis from 1 January 1995, and the Defendant was required to give one month's notice of termination of the Plaintiff's appointment prior to that date.
facts.F13: The Plaintiff was entitled to reimbursement for services rendered and expenses incurred prior to termination.
facts.F14: The Defendant did not provide one month's notice of termination, which would have been necessary as of 1 January 1995.

reference_issues: Whether the Defendant's termination of the Plaintiff's appointment was lawful
Whether the Plaintiff was entitled to damages for wrongful termination of the contract

claim: claiming damages for wrongful rejection of goods and storage fee
requested_remedy: claiming damages for wrongful rejection of goods and storage fee
parties: Defendant: WAN WOO FROZEN MEAT LIMITED

facts.F1: The plaintiff (Hopeful Meat) and the defendant (Wan Woo) have a long-standing business relationship in the trade of frozen meat in Hong Kong.
facts.F2: Hopeful Meat was the supplier of Wan Woo for more than 10 years prior to the commencement of these proceedings.
facts.F3: The dispute arose out of three sale transactions involving frozen chicken claws of the same Brazilian brand 'Corcovado' imported to Hong Kong.
facts.F4: The first transaction (First Invoice) involved 5 cartons of the goods and was delivered to Jackpot Company, the purchaser of Wan Woo, on or about 29 March 2011.
facts.F5: Wan Woo placed another order (Second Invoice) with Hopeful Meat on 31 March 2011, which involved 800 cartons of the goods.
facts.F6: Before the delivery of the goods under the Second Invoice, Wan Woo placed another order (Third Invoice) with Hopeful Meat on 2 April 2011, which involved 575 cartons of the goods.
facts.F7: Wan Woo rejected the delivery of 79 cartons of the goods under the Second Invoice and all 575 cartons of the goods under the Third Invoice due to the goods being smaller than those supplied under the First Invoice.
facts.F8: Hopeful Meat supplied goods from a company known as Sadia in Brazil to its parent company A.M.D. Co Limited (AMD).
facts.F9: The goods were supplied on the basis that they were unsized, and the code 'A4' used in the invoices refers to 'unsized goods'.
facts.F10: Hopeful Meat resold the rejected goods to other retailers and deducted the proceeds from Wan Woo's account.
facts.F11: Hopeful Meat demands Wan Woo to pay the shortfall and storage fee in the total sum of HK$111,682.50.
facts.F12: Au Yeung gave evidence that there was no discussion about the unit size of the goods to be supplied under the Second and Third Invoices.
facts.F13: A Report was compiled by Centralink Surveyors Ltd which the court found unreliable as it did not single out the goods delivered under the First Invoice and mixed them with other goods.

reference_issues: Whether the Second and Third Invoices evidenced sales by sample
Whether there was an express or implied term that the goods sold must correspond with those supplied under the First Invoice

Section 17 of the Sale of Goods Ordinance relating to sale by sample

facts.F10: The contracts required maintenance of the face value at a 5% level.

Whether the plaintiff had provided sufficient margin to cover the losses.

requested_remedy: The plaintiff claimed damages for personal injuries arising from a traffic accident on 4 April 1998, alleging that the defendant, as his employer, was in breach of his duty of care by refusing to allow the plaintiff to use the Lion Rock Tunnel as an alternative route, which the plaintiff considered safer due to the presence of wild monkeys on Tai Po Road.

facts.F1: The traffic accident occurred on 4 April 1998 when the plaintiff's lorry drove off Tai Po Road, crashed through a barrier, and overturned on Lung Cheung Road, causing the plaintiff severe injuries.
facts.F2: The plaintiff had been employed by the defendant as a driver cum delivery worker since December 1997.
facts.F3: The plaintiff's daily schedule involved making deliveries to various customers in the Shatin and Tai Wai areas, Kowloon, and Tsuen Wan.
facts.F4: The normal working hours for the plaintiff were from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. daily.
facts.F5: The plaintiff had previously seen other drivers almost having accidents due to monkeys on Tai Po Road and had a near-miss experience himself in March 1998.
facts.F6: The plaintiff informed the defendant and another employee, Yeung Chi, about the danger of monkeys on Tai Po Road and requested to use the Lion Rock Tunnel as an alternative route, which was denied by the defendant.
facts.F7: The plaintiff had to take evasive action when a monkey suddenly appeared on the road, leading to the accident.
facts.F8: The defendant operates a family business supplying frozen meat and has a place of business at Leader Industrial Centre in Shatin.
facts.F9: The plaintiff normally took Tai Po Road to make deliveries, as it was the most direct route, while the Lion Rock Tunnel would take an extra 10-15 minutes and involve tunnel charges.
facts.F10: The court considered Tai Po Road to be a normal, ordinary road with no additional hazards or risks beyond the usual risks faced by motorists on other roads in Hong Kong.
facts.F11: The defendant's refusal to allow the plaintiff to use the Lion Rock Tunnel as an alternative route was found to be not unreasonable.

reference_issues: Whether the defendant, as the plaintiff's employer, was in breach of his duty of care by refusing to allow the plaintiff to use the Lion Rock Tunnel as an alternative route.
Whether the plaintiff's fear of monkeys on Tai Po Road made the road any more hazardous than other roads in the territory.

facts.F1: On January 11, 1986, the plaintiff was working on the 7th floor of the Macau Ferry Terminal construction site when he fell through a gap on a platform made of loose planks resting on top of an air conditioning duct.
facts.F2: The plaintiff suffered serious injuries, including a fractured left femur and ankle, and a compression fracture of the fifth lumbar vertebra.
facts.F3: The construction site was managed by multiple contractors, with HIP HING CONSTRUCTION CO. LTD. as the plumbing and drainage sub-contractor, LUEN YICK WATER AND DRAINAGE WORKS LTD. as the principal contractor, and YOUNG’S ENGINEERING CO. LTD. as the air-conditioning sub-contractor.
facts.F4: The plaintiff was employed as a plumber by HIP HING CONSTRUCTION CO. LTD. and had received instructions from Fong Sing, a foreman, to rectify a water pipe on the 7th floor.
facts.F5: The air conditioning duct was installed and managed by YOUNG’S ENGINEERING CO. LTD.
facts.F6: The construction site had a standard practice of placing planks on top of ducts to prevent objects from falling in, but the planks in question were not securely attached.
facts.F7: D2 had provided safety equipment and taken steps to ensure its use by employees.
facts.F8: A proper working platform on the 7th floor was not provided by D2.

reference_issues: Was the defendant, HIP HING CONSTRUCTION CO. LTD. (D2), liable in negligence and breach of statutory duty under the regulations for failing to ensure the plaintiff’s safety?
Was the principal contractor, LUEN YICK WATER AND DRAINAGE WORKS LTD. (D1), liable as occupier under the Occupiers Liability Ordinance for failing to ensure the safety of the plaintiff?
Did the plaintiff contribute to his own injury through negligence?

claim: A sum of US$178,000 plus interest and costs
requested_remedy: A sum of US$178,000 plus interest and costs
parties: Defendant: David H. Woo trading as Phase Industries

facts.F1: The contract was made between Schmidt & Co. (Hong Kong) Ltd and Phase Industries on 10th July 1992 for the supply of Sillner Machines.
facts.F2: The contract included one set of a model BGM8 Embossed Tape Forming Machine, one set of a model CG4/02 Chip Taping Machine, and one set of a model system 940 Lumonics Laser Mark System.
facts.F3: The goods were to be delivered in Hangzhou C&F by air freight and were under German export control, subject to licence approval.
facts.F4: The Letter of Credit required partial delivery and allowed the air waybill to be accepted as evidence of delivery.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff and the Defendant were traders who knew relatively little about the machines and their construction.
facts.F6: The machine in question was designed to put very small computer chips onto a long sheet of plastic film.
facts.F7: The drawings for the parts were referred to as SOT-23 30-UP and were made by Kras Asia Ltd.
facts.F8: The parts had tight tolerances and required sophisticated mechanisms to measure them.
facts.F9: The machine was made by Sillner Maschinen GMBH in Germany.
facts.F10: Mr. Fidorra, a quality controller at Sillner Maschinen GMBH, tested the CG4/02 machine in Germany and found it to be working properly.
facts.F11: However, when the machine was installed in Hangzhou, there were difficulties with the CG4/02 machine.
facts.F12: The parts supplied were found to be defective, with bent leads, flashes, and gate remains.
facts.F13: The defective parts caused the machine to jam.
facts.F14: Mr. Woo argued that non-defective parts could have been used to test the machine, but this argument was rejected by the court.
facts.F15: A letter from Mr. Mento Lam of Kras Asia Ltd was submitted, but it was not considered to be sufficient evidence to support the Defendant's claim.
facts.F16: The Plaintiff did not insist on obtaining a Letter of Credit without the clause requiring a quality certificate.
facts.F17: The terms of the Letter of Credit required a quality certificate.

reference_issues: Whether the Plaintiff supplied what was required under the contract
Whether the machine was defective or if the parts supplied were defective
Whether the Plaintiff was entitled to its claim under the contract

claim: for the price of work done and damages for wrongful repudiation of a sub-contract
requested_remedy: for the price of work done and damages for wrongful repudiation of a sub-contract

facts.F1: The plaintiff (EU Asia) and the defendant (Wing Hong) entered into a subcontract agreement on 22nd December 1988.
facts.F2: Wing Hong was the Principal Contractor engaged by the Hong Kong Housing Authority to carry out certain building works.
facts.F3: The subcontract sum was $7,690,000.00.
facts.F4: Delays occurred, including delays in completing the lower floors, handing over the site, and the modification of the steel formwork.
facts.F5: The modification to the steel formwork was not completed until the middle or end of March 1989.
facts.F6: Wing Hong alleged that EU Asia failed to complete one whole storey within 9 working days, failed to carry out work in accordance with the progress under the main contract, and failed to make good honeycombing with due diligence.
facts.F7: EU Asia alleged that Wing Hong wrongfully repudiated the contract by preventing them from continuing with the works.
facts.F8: The court found that Wing Hong's witnesses, including Vincent Ho and Mr. Liu, were not credible, and their evidence was rejected.
facts.F9: The court accepted the evidence of EU Asia's witnesses, including Mr. Ng, Mr. Lee, Mr. Yu, and Mr. Chan.
facts.F10: The court found that EU Asia did not suspend work on the 4th and 5th May 1989, and that they were ready, willing, and able to carry out works, but were prevented from doing so by Wing Hong's failure to arrange inspection and order concrete.
facts.F11: The construction method for the upstand beams had to be approved by the Authority.
facts.F12: Honeycombing is a normal occurrence in construction and EU Asia would have made it good in the normal course of the work.
facts.F13: The value of work done by EU Asia at the date of termination was $273,497.00.
facts.F14: EU Asia suffered a loss of profit of $1,300,000.00 as a result of the wrongful repudiation of the contract.

reference_issues: Whether Wing Hong had the right to determine the contract on 6th May 1989.
Whether EU Asia had breached the contract by failing to complete one whole storey within 9 working days.
Whether EU Asia had breached the contract by failing to carry out work in accordance with the progress under the main contract.
Whether EU Asia had breached the contract by failing to make good honeycombing with due diligence.
The value of work done by EU Asia and the amount of loss of profit suffered by them as a result of the wrongful repudiation of the contract.

claim: Damages for misrepresentation and/or breach of warranty arising from the purchase of a Mercedes Benz S430 motor car
requested_remedy: Damages for misrepresentation and/or breach of warranty arising from the purchase of a Mercedes Benz S430 motor car

facts.F1: Gavin Watson, the Plaintiff's managing director, and his friend Stephen Mansfield visited the Defendant's motor car showroom in Gloucester Road, Wanchai, on 6th May 2000.
facts.F2: Mr. Watson was highly knowledgeable about motor cars and was looking for a car for his wife, saw a Mercedes Benz S320 which seemed suitable, and spoke to the salesman, Mr. Michael Wong.
facts.F3: Mr. Watson was aware that the Defendant was not a Mercedes Benz authorised dealer and was keen to establish the provenance of the car, specifically that it was a brand new car manufactured in 2000.
facts.F4: Mr. Wong confirmed that the S320 was a 2000 model and had been imported directly from Germany, and later agreed to provide the Mercedes Benz S430, which had a larger engine, as an alternative option.
facts.F5: Mr. Watson purchased the S430 on 12th May 2000, with a purchase agreement describing the car as a 'Brand New 2000 M. Benz S430L' with a purchase price of $1,040,000.
facts.F6: The car was eventually delivered on 19th June 2000, with an invoice from AGA Motors describing the car as a 'Brand New 2000 M. Benz S430L'.
facts.F7: In August 2001, Mr. Watson took the car to Zung Fu, the authorised Mercedes Benz dealer, for servicing, and later received a letter stating that the date of manufacture of the car was 18th December 1998, not 2000.
facts.F8: The car had a complete electrical breakdown, and Mr. Watson sold it to a motor dealer for $490,000 on 8th February 2002.
facts.F9: A valuer, Mr. Raymond Lee, valued the car between $500,000 and $520,000, assuming it was a 1998 model, and between $680,000 and $700,000 if it were a 2000 model.
facts.F10: Mr. Watson relied on Mr. Wong's statement about the car's age in making the purchase.
facts.F11: The car was not manufactured in 2000, but in 1998.

reference_issues: Whether the Defendant made a misrepresentation about the age of the car
Whether the misrepresentation was a warranty
Whether the Plaintiff is entitled to damages for breach of warranty

claim: The Plaintiff claims damages under the Misrepresentation Ordinance (Cap. 284) and consequential losses.
requested_remedy: The Plaintiff claims damages under the Misrepresentation Ordinance (Cap. 284) and consequential losses.
parties: Defendant: PHOENIX LUMBER NICARAGUA S.A., PHOENIX LUMBER S.A., HIMANSHU GIRDHAR DUA

facts.F1: The North Atlantic Autonomous Region (R.A.A.N.) of Nicaragua is the largest territory in Nicaragua, comprising a large jungle that goes from the mountain and valleys of the Northern and Central region to the coast of the Caribbean Sea.
facts.F2: In 2007, Hurricane Felix hit the region and forest areas were destroyed. Logging operations by timber operators were permitted to commence in affected areas to extract timber subject to local regulations.
facts.F3: The agreement that is the subject matter of these proceedings relates to an opportunity to participate in such logging operations in Nicaragua.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff is an investment company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands and the 1st and 2nd Defendants are private companies incorporated in Nicaragua.
facts.F5: The 3rd Defendant is an individual and his role and position are disputed.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff asserts that the 3rd Defendant held himself out as a director and shareholder of the 2nd Defendant and made representations pre-contract and post-contract prior to completion of the terms of the agreement upon which reliance was placed by the Plaintiff.
facts.F7: The 3rd Defendant denies the Plaintiff's assertions and avers that he believed himself to be a director and shareholder of the 2nd Defendant but was informed that he had not been validly appointed as a director of the 1st and 2nd Defendants and nor had any shareholding in the 2nd Defendant been allotted to him.
facts.F8: The parties entered into an Asset Purchase and Sale Agreement on or about 19 August 2010.
facts.F9: The Plaintiff claims that it had been induced into the agreement by false pre-contract and pre-completion representations made by the 3rd Defendant.
facts.F10: The 3rd Defendant denies that the Plaintiff was induced into the agreement by such representations and avers that the representations were true and accurate at the time they were made.
facts.F11: The Court considered the expert evidence on Nicaraguan law.
facts.F12: The Court reviewed the documents created by the parties.

reference_issues: What was the role of the 3rd Defendant in the dealings with the Plaintiff in respect of the Nicaraguan timber project?
Whether the 3rd Defendant made, repeated, adopted and/or ratified the pre-contract and pre-completion representations?
Whether the pre-contract and pre-completion representations were false and made fraudulently?
Whether the Plaintiff relied on the pre-contract and pre-completion representations in entering into the agreement and proceeding to completion under the agreement?
Whether the false pre-contract and pre-completion representations caused the Plaintiff to suffer loss and damage and if so what is their proper assessment?
Whether the Plaintiff failed to mitigate its loss?

claim: The Plaintiff alleged that the Defendant was in breach of statutory duties and negligent as an employer, resulting in the Plaintiff's injury
requested_remedy: The Plaintiff alleged that the Defendant was in breach of statutory duties and negligent as an employer, resulting in the Plaintiff's injury
parties: Defendant: TAI LEE CAFÉ & CAKE SHOP (a firm)

facts.F1: The Plaintiff was a chef working at the Defendant's restaurant in Tuen Mun.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff alleged that he was injured on 15/2/2004 while pouring boiled soup from a pot to a plastic container, but the Defendant denied the alleged accident ever happened.
facts.F3: The Plaintiff had worked for the Defendant for about 3 years before the alleged accident.
facts.F4: The Plaintiff normally used a metal ladle to transfer the boiled soup but it was broken on the day of the alleged accident.
facts.F5: The Plaintiff attempted to transfer the boiled soup by directly pouring it from the pot to the plastic container without using a ladle.
facts.F6: The Plaintiff used a cotton towel to insulate his left hand against the heat of the pot, but the pot slipped and he sprained his wrist.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff continued working for the whole day despite the injury and only went to the Accident & Emergency Department of Tuen Mun Hospital to seek consultation after 11 pm.
facts.F8: The Plaintiff was given sick leaves from 15 to 18/2/2004.
facts.F9: The Defendant's person-in-charge of the kitchen, Mr. Cheung, had informed the Defendant about the broken ladle a few days before the alleged accident but the Defendant did not provide another ladle for replacement.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff had been suffering from non-specific synovitis of multiple joints on his right hand before the alleged accident.
facts.F11: There was at least one ladle or utensil in the kitchen suitable for use by the Plaintiff to transfer soup at the time.
facts.F12: The Plaintiff went to the Accident & Emergency Department of Tuen Mun Hospital after 11 pm on the day of the alleged accident.
facts.F13: The court reviewed the hospital records in reaching its decision.

reference_issues: Whether the alleged accident happened on 15/2/2004
Whether the Defendant was in breach of statutory duties and negligent as an employer
Whether the Plaintiff was injured due to his own illness or the alleged accident

claim: claims for US$2,259,900.33 on goods delivered before 1 April 2004, US$1,588,554.18 on orders cancelled by Team Products on 1 April 2004, and US$281,428 on goods despatched from a factory to Team Products on 4 and 10 April 2004
requested_remedy: claims for US$2,259,900.33 on goods delivered before 1 April 2004, US$1,588,554.18 on orders cancelled by Team Products on 1 April 2004, and US$281,428 on goods despatched from a factory to Team Products on 4 and 10 April 2004
parties: Plaintiff: CellPlus (H K) Limited, Shenzhen Envirotec Electronics Co Ltd

Defendant: Team Products International, Inc, SU ZHAN HAO (also known as JOHN SU), Wang Ching Feng (also known as DEBBIE WANG FEUERSTEIN), Shenzhen Honesty Electronics Co Ltd, Shenzhen Envirotec Electronics Co Ltd

facts.F1: CellPlus claims for payment from Team Products for goods delivered and despatched but not paid for.
facts.F2: Team Products defends the claim, arguing it was misled by CellPlus about its manufacturing capacity and raising issues with cancelling orders and disputed prices.
facts.F3: The case involves associated companies Shenzhen Honesty Electronics Co. Ltd. (Honesty), Envirotec Asia Limited (Envirotec-HK), and Shenzhen Envirotec Electronics Co. Ltd. (Envirotec-PRC).
facts.F4: A course of business had developed where Team Products ordered goods from CellPlus, who would place corresponding orders with Envirotec-PRC, which would then ship finished goods to Team Products.
facts.F5: The exact terms and shareholding agreement between Mr. Su and Ms. Wang in Envirotec-PRC are disputed.
facts.F6: Envirotec-PRC was formed to manufacture pest repellers ordered by Team Products.
facts.F7: An alleged representation about CellPlus entering into a joint venture to manufacture goods is scrutinized for making a false statement.
facts.F8: There was a shipment of goods from a factory to Team Products on 4 and 10 April 2004.
facts.F9: No evidence of goods being shipped on board a vessel was provided by CellPlus to meet its delivery obligation under the FOB contract.

lawsuit_type: action for payment and interim judgment
reference_issues: Was there an actionable misrepresentation made by CellPlus about its manufacturing capacity and joint venture?
Did Team Products validly cancel orders and avoid payment, or did the purported cancellation constitute a breach of contract?
Were goods despatched from the factory but not received by Team Products, and did CellPlus fulfill its delivery obligation?
Is Team Products entitled to a legal set-off for Volume Incentive Rebate (VIR) against any sum due to CellPlus?

claim: arrears of rent amounting to $2,767,043.00
requested_remedy: arrears of rent amounting to $2,767,043.00

facts.F1: The Plaintiff and the Defendant entered into a Tenancy Agreement for the residential premises known as Canberra Villa, Hang Lok Lane, Tung Lo Wan Hill, Shatin.
facts.F2: The tenancy was for 3 years commencing 28 November 1996 and the monthly rent was HK$138,000.00.
facts.F3: The Defendant operated the premises as a rest home.
facts.F4: In August 1997, the Defendant asked for a reduction in rent due to financial difficulties and the Plaintiff agreed to reduce the rent by $10,000.00 p.m. for 3 months.
facts.F5: The Defendant took advantage of the concession and paid the reduced rate for 5 months without the Plaintiff's consent.
facts.F6: On 8-2-98, a mudslide occurred near the access road leading to the premises and the road was closed to vehicular traffic.
facts.F7: The Defendant was unable to operate the rest home and claimed she had an oral agreement with the Plaintiff to pay reduced rent of $50,000.00 p.m. until the road reopened and she was permitted to resume business.
facts.F8: The Plaintiff denied any such agreement and claimed that the Defendant's payment of reduced rent was without its consent.
facts.F9: The Defendant vacated the premises in March 1999 and the Plaintiff inspected the premises and found that they had not been reinstated as required by the Tenancy Agreement.
facts.F10: The Plaintiff claimed that the Defendant had removed kitchen and bathroom fittings and had not replaced them.
facts.F11: The Plaintiff sent a letter of demand through its solicitors to the Defendant.
facts.F12: The evidence established the Defendant's failure to replace the water heater and baths, but not the reinstatement of the toilet and kitchen.
facts.F13: The amount adjudged to be owed by the Defendant was set-off against the deposit of $690,000.00.

reference_issues: Whether there was an oral agreement between the parties for a reduced rent.
Whether the Plaintiff had waived its right to full rental for the period during which the partial payments were made.
Whether the deposit of $690,000.00 was reasonable and whether it should be forfeited.

claim: consultancy fees outstanding for services rendered in the sum of $243,095
requested_remedy: consultancy fees outstanding for services rendered in the sum of $243,095

facts.F1: The Plaintiff is a chartered quantity surveyor with 40 years of construction industry experience.
facts.F2: The Defendant is a construction contractor in underground drainage works.
facts.F3: The Incorporated Owners of Vista Panorama awarded to the Defendant a contract for underground drainage works at Vista Panorama on 7th July 2001.
facts.F4: The contract price was $990,000 including a provisional sum of $486,190.
facts.F5: The parties further agreed that the Defendant would perform a CCTV survey report and replace all underground drainage pipes at the $990,000 lump sum.
facts.F6: Preliminary approval was obtained on or about 5th November 2001.
facts.F7: Written instructions for such works were issued on 11th January 2002.
facts.F8: The Defendant retained the Plaintiff as a consultant for the said contract in or about August 2001 at a flat fee of $3,500 per month.
facts.F9: The Plaintiff supplied services to the Defendant between 19th December 2001 and 18th June 2002.
facts.F10: The Defendant was paid the $990,000 for the work done under the contract certified by a payment certificate dated 11th October 2002 and no further sums were paid under the contract.
facts.F11: Evidence of Mr. Wong supported the Defendant's understanding of the 2nd agreement.
facts.F12: Mr. Chang would pursue payment of an extra $486,190 over and above the lump sum contract price of $990,000 rather than the recovery or avoidance of deduction of the said contract sum.

reference_issues: What was the contract between the Employer and the Defendant?
What was the agreement between the Employer and the Defendant regarding the provisional sum of $486,190?
What were in the minds of the Plaintiff and Mr. Chan when they reached the 7th and 20th February 2002 agreement (the 2nd agreement)?
Is the 2nd agreement between the Plaintiff and the Defendant enforceable?

claim: claims that 2 large sums of money which it had invested in a Fund in 2018 and 2019 were not used for that purpose and seeks damages and tracing remedies against the Defendants based on misrepresentation, breach of contract, inducing breach of contract, unlawful means conspiracy, negligence, unjust enrichment, knowing receipt and dishonest assistance
requested_remedy: claims that 2 large sums of money which it had invested in a Fund in 2018 and 2019 were not used for that purpose and seeks damages and tracing remedies against the Defendants based on misrepresentation, breach of contract, inducing breach of contract, unlawful means conspiracy, negligence, unjust enrichment, knowing receipt and dishonest assistance

facts.F1: The Plaintiff had invested two large sums of money in a Fund in 2018 and 2019.
facts.F2: The Plaintiff obtained an ex parte proprietary injunction against, inter alia, D7 in respect of the said sums of money on 27th April 2021.
facts.F3: The Plaintiff took out an inter parte Summons for the continuation of the ex parte order and for ancillary disclosure (Summons (1)) on 29 April 2021.
facts.F4: D7 took out a Summons to discharge the ex parte order on 6 May 2021 and offered an undertaking in place of the injunction (Summons (2)).
facts.F5: D7 produced evidence showing that the traceable proceeds of the Plaintiff’s money were limited to a sum of US$967,927.08.
facts.F6: At the hearing of Summons (2) on 7 May 2021, it was ordered that the substantive argument be heard on 18 May 2021.
facts.F7: The Plaintiff took out another Summons for various relief (Summons (3)) on 12 May 2021.
facts.F8: At the hearing on 18 May 2021, D7’s undertaking to preserve the Sum was accepted by the court and the injunction was discharged.
facts.F9: The Summons (3) Relief were adjourned for argument.
facts.F10: On 6 January 2022, the Plaintiff gave notice to D7 that those Relief are no longer pursued.
facts.F11: D7 denies each of the claims against it and claims to be an innocent custodian, asserting a positive claim to the Sum as fees for its custodian and related duties.
facts.F12: The costs arguments are disproportionate.
facts.F13: The Sum can be traced to the Plaintiff's investment in the Fund.

lawsuit_type: costs in relation to three Summonses
reference_issues: The court's approach to costs in relation to the three Summonses
Whether D7 is entitled to costs on an indemnity basis due to material non-disclosure
Whether the Plaintiff is barred from opening up the injunction by relying on the Chanel principle
